source_text: Ξενιζέσθω δὲ μηδεὶς εἰ τὴν θανάτῳ καὶ φθορᾷ διακοπτομένην ζωὴν ὀνομάζομεν διαμονήν, λογιζόμενος ὡς οὐχ εἷς τοῦ προσρήματος ὁ λόγος, οὐχ ἓν τῆς διαμονῆς τὸ μέτρον, ὅτι μηδὲ τῶν διαμενόντων φύσις μία. Εἴπερ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν φύσιν ἕκαστον τῶν διαμενόντων ἔχει τὴν διαμονήν, οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν καθαρῶς ἀφθάρτων καὶ ἀθανάτων εὕροι τις ἂν ἰσάζουσαν τὴν διαμονήν, τῷ μηδὲ τὰς οὐσίας τῶν κρειττόνων συνεξισοῦσθαι ταῖς καθ᾿ ὑπόβασιν διαφερούσαις, οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὴν ὁμαλὴν ἐκείνην τὴν ἀμετάβλητον ἐπιζητεῖν ἄξιον, ἅτε δὴ τῶν μὲν ἐξ ἀρχῆς γενομένων ἀθανάτων καὶ διαμενόντων μόνῃ τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἀτελευτήτως, τῶν δὲ ἀνθρώπων κατὰ μὲν τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ γενέσεως ἐχόντων τὴν ἀμετάβλητον διαμονήν, κατὰ δὲ τὸ σῶμα προσλαμβανόντων ἐκ μεταβολῆς τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν· ὅπερ ὁ τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγος βούλεται· πρὸς ἣν ἀποβλέποντες, τήν τε διάλυσιν τοῦ σώματος, ὡς ἑπομένην τῇ μετ᾿ ἐνδείας καὶ φθορᾶς ζωῇ, περιμένομεν, καὶ μετὰ ταύτην τὴν μετ᾿ ἀφθαρσίας ἐλπίζομεν διαμονήν, οὔτε τῇ τῶν ἀλόγων τελευτῇ συνεξισοῦντες τὴν ἡμετέραν τελευτήν, οὔτε τῇ τῶν ἀθανάτων διαμονῇ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων διαμονήν, ἵνα μὴ λάθωμεν ταύτῃ συνεξισοῦντες καὶ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν καὶ ζωὴν οἷς μὴ προσῆκεν. Οὐ τοίνυν ἐπὶ τούτῳ δυσχεραίνειν ἄξιον, εἴ τις ἀνωμαλία θεωρεῖται περὶ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων διαμονήν, οὐδ᾿ ἐπειδὴ χωρισμὸς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τῶν τοῦ σώματος μερῶν καὶ μορίων διάλυσις τὴν συνεχῆ διακόπτει ζωήν, διὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἀπογινώσκειν χρὴ τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐπειδὴ τὴν κατὰ συναίσθησιν ζωὴν διακόπτειν δοκοῦσιν αἱ κατὰ τὸν ὕπνον φυσικῶς ἐγγινόμεναι παρέσεις τῶν αἰσθήσεων καὶ τῶν φυσικῶν δυνάμεων, ἰσομέτροις χρόνου διαστήμασιν ὑπνούντων τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ τρόπον τινὰ πάλιν ἀναβιωσκόντων, τὴν αὐτὴν παραιτούμεθα ζωὴν λέγειν· παρ᾿ ἣν αἰτίαν, οἶμαι, τινὲς ἀδελφὸν τοῦ θανάτου τὸν ὕπνον ὀνομάζουσιν, οὐχ ὡς ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν προγόνων ἢ πατέρων φύντας γενεαλογοῦντες, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς τῶν ὁμοίων παθῶν τοῖς τε θανοῦσι καὶ τοῖς ὑπνοῦσιν ἐγγινομένων, ἕνεκά γε τῆς ἠρεμίας καὶ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἐπαισθάνεσθαι τῶν παρόντων ἢ γινομένων, μᾶλλον δὲ μηδὲ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ τῆς ἰδίας ζωῆς. Εἴπερ οὖν τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ζωὴν τοσαύτης γέμουσαν ἀνωμαλίας ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, καὶ διακοπτομένην πᾶσιν οἷς προείπομεν, οὐ παραιτούμεθα τὴν αὐτὴν λέγειν ζωήν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐπέκεινα τῆς διαλύσεως ζωήν, ἥτις ἑαυτῇ συνεισάγει τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἀπογινώσκειν ὀφείλομεν, κἂν ἐπὶ ποσὸν διακόπτηται τῷ χωρισμῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος.
thought_title: Sleep as a model for interrupted life
orientation: Athenagoras is answering the objection that death interrupts life, so resurrection cannot restore the same life; he argues that human life is already marked by interruptions such as sleep, yet we still call it one life.
pass_a_gloss: Let no one be surprised if the life being cut short by death and corruption we call continuance, reckoning that not one is the account of the appellation, not one the measure of the continuance, because not even of the things that continue is the nature one. For if according to its own nature each of the things that continue has the continuance, neither in the case of the purely incorruptible and immortal things would one find equal continuance, because not even the substances of the better things are made equal to the things differing by descent, nor in the case of humans is it fitting to seek that smooth and unchangeable [continuance], since indeed the things made from the beginning immortal and continuing endlessly by the purpose alone of the maker, but humans according to the soul from birth having the unchangeable continuance, but according to the body receiving in addition from change the incorruptibility; which very thing the account of the resurrection intends; looking toward which, both the dissolution of the body, as following the life with want and corruption, we await, and after this the continuance with incorruptibility we hope for, neither making equal our death to the death of the irrational animals, nor the continuance of humans to the continuance of the immortals, lest we escape notice by this making equal both the nature and life of humans to things to which it did not belong. Not therefore at this is it fitting to be annoyed, if some irregularity is observed concerning the continuance of humans, nor since separation of soul from the parts and members of the body [and] dissolution cuts short the continuous life, for this reason must one despair of the resurrection. For not even since the life according to perception seem to cut short the relaxations of the senses and of the natural powers occurring naturally in sleep, with equal measures of intervals of time humans sleeping and in some way again coming back to life, do we decline to call it the same life; for which cause, I think, some call sleep the brother of death, not as from the same ancestors or fathers sprung [ones] genealogizing, but as of similar affections occurring to both the dead and the sleeping, on account of the rest and of the perceiving nothing of the things present or happening, and rather not even of being and of one's own life. If therefore the life of humans, so full of irregularity from birth until dissolution, and cut short by all the things which we have said before, we do not decline to call the same life, neither the life beyond the dissolution, which brings in with itself the resurrection, ought we to despair of, even if for some time it is cut short by the separation of the soul from the body.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'continuance' for διαμονή, and the argument hinges on distinguishing different kinds of continuance.
The verb διακόπτω means to cut through or interrupt; 'cut short' captures the interruption of life by death and corruption.
The glossary requires 'incorruptibility' for ἀφθαρσία, distinguishing the risen body's state from mere immortality.
The phrase is a known proverb; keeping 'brother' preserves the familial metaphor that Athenagoras immediately corrects.
The compound verb emphasizes joint or mutual equalizing; 'making equal' keeps the force of the comparison Athenagoras rejects.
The term means unevenness or irregularity; it is central to the argument that human life is not uniform but marked by interruptions.

pass_b_english: No one should be surprised if we call a life that is cut short by death and decay a continuance. The word does not mean one thing, and continuance does not have one measure, because the things that continue do not have one nature. Each thing that continues has its continuance according to its own nature. So among things that are purely incorruptible and immortal you would not find an equal continuance, since the substances of the higher beings are not made equal to those that differ by being inferior. Nor is it right to demand for human beings that smooth, unchanging continuance.

The beings that existed from the beginning are immortal and continue endlessly by the purpose of their Maker alone. Human beings, however, have an unchanging continuance in soul from birth, but in body they receive incorruptibility in addition through change. This is what the doctrine of the resurrection intends. Looking toward it, we await the dissolution of the body, since it follows a life marked by need and decay, and after that we hope for a continuance with incorruptibility. We do not make our death equal to the death of irrational animals, nor do we make the continuance of human beings equal to the continuance of the immortals. Otherwise we would without realizing it make human nature and life equal to things to which they do not belong.

So it is not right to be troubled if some irregularity is observed in the continuance of human beings. Nor, because the separation of the soul from the parts and members of the body and their dissolution cuts short continuous life, should we for that reason despair of the resurrection. Sleep brings natural relaxations of the senses and natural powers, and people sleep for measured intervals of time and then in a way come back to life. We do not refuse to call this the same life, even though these relaxations seem to cut short the life of conscious awareness. For this reason, I think, some call sleep the brother of death. They are not tracing a genealogy as if the two were born from the same ancestors or parents, but because similar experiences come to those who have died and those who sleep: the stillness, the lack of awareness of what is present or happening, and not even awareness of being or of one's own life.

Human life is full of so much irregularity from birth to dissolution, and it is cut short by all the things we have mentioned. Yet we do not refuse to call it the same life. So we ought not to despair of the life beyond dissolution, which brings the resurrection with it, even if it is cut short for a time by the separation of the soul from the body.

problems.why: ὑπόβασις means 'diminution/decline,' not 'descent.' The contrast is between higher beings and those that differ by being inferior/lesser, not genealogical descent.
problems.fix: those that differ by being inferior
problems.ruling: καθ᾿ ὑπόβασιν means 'by inferiority/decline,' not 'descent'; misleading contrast with higher beings.

problems.quote: the lack of awareness of being and of one's own life
problems.source_quote: μηδὲ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ τῆς ἰδίας ζωῆς
problems.why: μηδὲ is 'not even,' not 'and even more.' The Greek intensifies to complete unawareness of existence itself, not a lesser awareness.
problems.fix: not even awareness of being or of one's own life
problems.ruling: μηδὲ means 'not even,' intensifying to unawareness of existence; 'even more' reverses the escalation.
